nameStory: The Iceland Necklace-shell gets its name from its northern Atlantic distribution, where it was first discovered around Iceland's waters. The 'necklace-shell' part comes from its smooth, rounded shell that resembles a polished bead you might string on a necklace. It's also called the Iceland moonsnail, linking it to its moon snail family relatives.
description: The Iceland Necklace-shell is a predatory sea snail that belongs to the moon snail family. Like its relatives, it has a smooth, rounded shell with a glossy surface that can range from pale cream to light brown. This marine mollusk is a hunter, using its large muscular foot to burrow through sand and mud in search of clams and other shellfish to eat. It's relatively uncommon in New England waters, making it an exciting find for beachcombers.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Look for a distinctly rounded, globe-like shell that feels smooth and solid in your hand, similar to a large marble

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: The shell typically appears cream to light brown with a glossy, polished finish that almost seems to glow

idTips.label: Opening Size
idTips.description: The shell opening (aperture) is large and oval-shaped, taking up about half the shell's height

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The shell feels completely smooth to the touch with no ridges, bumps, or rough patches

idTips.label: Shell Weight
idTips.description: Despite its size, the shell feels surprisingly heavy and solid for its size when held

habitat: Iceland Necklace-shells live in deeper offshore waters along New England's coast, typically on sandy or muddy sea floors. You're most likely to find their empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, especially along the Maine coast and outer Cape Cod. They prefer colder waters and are much rarer than their common moon snail cousins.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash ashore after winter storms, appearing fresh and glossy on the beach. Look for them among other storm debris in the wrack line.
seasonality.summer: Beach searching is most productive during calm periods when you can spot shells that haven't been tumbled by heavy surf. The shells will have their most vibrant coloring.
seasonality.fall: Storm season brings the best chance of finding shells as rough seas stir up deeper waters. Check beaches after nor'easters for the freshest specimens.
seasonality.winter: While harsh conditions make beach combing challenging, winter storms can uncover shells that have been buried in sand for months.

funFact: Iceland Necklace-shells are such effective predators that they can drill perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other mollusks using a specialized rasping tongue called a radula, essentially turning their prey's own shell into a lid they can't close!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the much more common Northern Moon Snail, but Iceland Necklace-shells have a more perfectly round, globe-like shape and glossier finish. Remember: if it looks like a polished marble, it's likely the rarer Iceland species; if it's more egg-shaped and duller, it's probably a moon snail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called both 'necklace-shell' and 'moonsnail,' this species is technically in a different genus (Amauropsis) than the true moon snails (Lunaria), though they're in the same family and have very similar lifestyles and appearances.
compareHints: Since there are no other Amauropsis species in New England waters, compare it to Northern Moon Snails in the Lunaria genus. Iceland Necklace-shells are more perfectly spherical and have a shinier, more polished appearance, while Northern Moon Snails tend to be more egg-shaped with a duller, more matte finish. The Iceland species also tends to be found in slightly deeper, colder waters.
